source.title: PURE: Turning Polysemantic Neurons Into Pure Features by Identifying Relevant Circuits
source.authors: Maximilian Dreyer; Erblina Purelku; Johanna Vielhaben; W. Samek; S. Lapuschkin

page_placements.theme: Shares of interpretable or polysemantic units outside language models (vision CNNs, ViT/CLIP, audio, tabular, CT encoders)

record.file_problem: The paper text and appendix are present, but plots are garbled or flattened, so their numerical values cannot be recovered.
record.tranche_reason: It evaluates a different neuron-disentangling method against activation-based clustering using CLIP-based interpretability measures, bearing on the claim that better tools improve neuron interpretability.
record.gate_note: The study reports results about ResNet neuron clustering and interpretability. It does not report Qwen neuron-pole shares, results on language models, held-out activation prediction, automated explanation scores, or attribution graphs explaining model behavior. Cited findings from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: This is a method paper. PURE splits ResNet penultimate-layer neurons into 'virtual' neurons by clustering circuit attributions. Nearly every result compares PURE with activation-based clustering on CLIP and DINOv2 distance proxies. That is the study's own method against others: it gives no share of interpretable neurons, no language models and no attribution-graph or held-out prediction test. So it does not test V4 or any other version. A side observation that most ResNet-50 neurons look fairly monosemantic is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that PURE splits polysemantic ResNet neurons into purer virtual neurons, yielding more purified features than activation-based clustering by CLIP/DINOv2 evaluation. They note that foundation-model embeddings are only a proxy for human interpretability, and leave human evaluation and ablations to future work.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses partial-backward-pass Gradient×Activation attributions and k-means to assign circuits, then evaluates feature clusters with CLIP and DINOv2 on ImageNet ResNets. It does not perform the Qwen neuron-pole audit described in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Cluster count changes the distance pattern: higher k generally lowers intra-cluster distances, while inter-cluster distances often decrease. The study also reports architecture-dependent distributions and selected neurons where PURE clustering diverges from CLIP.

fits_no_version.finding: In ImageNet ResNet-50, CLIP-based 2-cluster analysis of penultimate-layer neurons shows that only a few hundred of 2048 neurons have large separation, i.e. are polysemantic. The authors say most neurons are 'rather monosemantic'. ResNet-34 appears less polysemantic than ResNet-101 (tentative).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In ImageNet ResNets' penultimate layers, judged by CLIP-embedding clustering of top-activating crops, most neurons are largely monosemantic and a minority (roughly 10–20% in ResNet-50) encode clearly separable distinct features.

record.problems: Interpretability is evaluated using CLIP and DINOv2 as proxies; the authors say human feedback or controlled evaluation would be valuable. The analysis is limited to penultimate-layer ImageNet ResNets, uses a fixed clustering procedure in the main setup, and reports some results only in plots whose numerical values are not recoverable here.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible reported result was intentionally left out. Numerical plot values are recorded as figure only where the plotted values are not recoverable.

untested.parts: The Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit and its shares of one-job, two-job and not-yet-understood poles.
Any language model, dense or mixture-of-experts, and scale.
InceptionV1 cat/car and other canonical polysemantic neurons; the recursive-generalization reading.

Any share of interpretable neurons and whether it rises with better tools or modern architectures. Causes such as architecture or regularization. InceptionV1-sized estimates. PURE creates virtual neurons rather than showing that the original neurons are interpretable.
Neuron-based attribution graphs explaining model behaviour without a replacement model.
Whether explanations from activating examples predict firing on held-out inputs.
Simulation-based automated scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' and V4 'supports' labels are withdrawn. Comparing the study's own disentangling method against a baseline on proxy metrics does not show that the share of interpretable neurons rises with tools. The paper's framing assumes genuine polysemanticity that needs splitting, which is closer to the opposite of V3/V4's spirit, but it offers no direct test of those versions. The authors also note that CLIP can separate samples the model treats as one semantics (neuron #271), a caveat on the proxy.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B audit and the stated shares of one-job, two-job, and not-yet-understood neuron poles.
Language models, dense versus mixture-of-experts models, and model scale up to trillions of parameters.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car examples, pose detection, and recursive generalization.

The study tests interpretability-tool comparisons in ResNets, but not the proposed causes involving architecture or regularization, nor the InceptionV1-sized estimates or a percentage of neurons rendered interpretable.
Whether attribution graphs built from a model's own neurons explain model behavior without a replacement model or reconstruction error.
Whether explanations based on activating examples predict where neurons fire on held-out examples.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulated activations on new text.

rows.subject: ResNet-50
rows.operation_detail: Cluster each neuron's 100 most activating samples into two groups and compare CLIP embedding distances.
rows.measure: Change in CLIP visual-feature distances after clustering
rows.value: For most neurons clustering improves visual similarity; a few hundred of the 2048 neurons show a larger improvement.
rows.note: The paper treats larger improvements as indicating more polysemantic neurons; it does not state an interpretable-neuron percentage.
rows.check: Distribution of polysemanticity in ResNet-50: a few hundred of 2048 neurons show large cluster separation. This uses a CLIP proxy in a vision model and involves no tool comparison, so it fits no version as stated; moved to fits_no_version. The baseline is overall distance before clustering, and the 'partial' state was not meaningful for V4.

rows.subject: ResNet-50
rows.operation_detail: Compare PURE-attribution clustering with clustering based on CLIP embeddings for selected neurons.
rows.measure: Agreement between PURE clustering and CLIP clustering of feature visualizations
rows.value: PURE clustering can diverge from CLIP; for neuron #271, CLIP separates dogs from windmills although the paper says they share a triangular-shape semantics.
rows.note: The authors also describe attribution clusters that differ from CLIP for neurons #614 and #1055, and abstract features that are difficult to interpret.
rows.check: Qualitative examples where PURE clustering diverges from CLIP for ResNet-50 neurons. This concerns the validity of the evaluation proxy, not a V4 effect.

rows.operation_detail: Vary the number of clusters used to create virtual neurons.
rows.value: As k increases, intra-cluster distances are generally lower, while inter-cluster distance often decreases.
rows.note: This trend is stated across experiments rather than as separate numerical results for each model.
rows.check: Effect of the number of clusters k on distances. This is a property of the method; the authors read falling inter-cluster distance as most neurons being monosemantic. It is not a V4 measure.

relation.reason: It comments on how common polysemantic neurons are ('most neurons are rather monosemantic') but tests no version.

tranche.reason: This is a method paper. PURE uses lower-layer neuron attributions as circuit units and mainly reports its own method against activation-based clustering. The polysemanticity distribution in A.2 is a CLIP-proxy side observation on ImageNet ResNets and gives no interpretable-neuron share, so it fits no version.

source_check.notes: This is a vision study (ImageNet ResNet-34/50/101, penultimate layer). Polysemanticity is judged only by a CLIP-embedding cluster-separation proxy, with no human audit and no stated share. R17's model is ResNet-101, not ResNet-100.

statements.correction: A.2 (ResNet-50, k=2 on CLIP embeddings of the 100 top samples): 'a few hundred of the 2048 neurons' show larger improvement, read as more polysemantic. A.4: inter-cluster distance often falls as k rises, 'most neurons are rather monosemantic'.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: PURE versus activation-based clustering on the tested ResNet models and cluster settings, using CLIP-based visual separation and alignment measures
reader_labels.reason: The reported CLIP measures favor PURE over activation-based clustering, though they do not establish a rise in the fraction of human-interpretable neurons (R01-R15).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Selected ResNet-50 neurons and varying cluster counts
reader_labels.reason: PURE clusters sometimes diverge from CLIP, and increasing cluster count can lower inter-cluster distance; the study does not validate the measures against human judgments (R18-R19).
